parts.title: The volcano in the kitchen
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last year, I decided to enter our school science competition with a project about volcanoes. My plan was simple: I would build a model volcano in the garden and make it erupt with baking soda, vinegar and red food colour. I read about it online, I watched three videos, and I felt sure that nothing could go wrong.

On the day before the competition, I tested the volcano in the kitchen, because it was raining outside. My mother was at work, and I thought I would tidy everything up before she came home. I mixed the baking soda and vinegar, and a small red river began to run down the side. It looked wonderful. Then I decided that it was not big enough, and I added another cup of vinegar.

The next minute was a disaster. Red foam shot up to the ceiling, ran across the table and fell onto the floor. The dog, who had been sleeping in his basket, woke up and started to bark. When my mother arrived home, I was kneeling on the floor with a mop, covered in red from head to foot.

She was not angry, to my surprise, and she even helped me to clean up. Next day, I took a smaller volcano to school, and it worked perfectly. I came second, and the judges said that my explanation was the clearest. But the story that everybody remembers is the one about the kitchen.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer feel confident about her project?
options: She had a teacher to help her.
She had won a prize before.
questions.explanation: She read about it online and watched three videos, so she felt sure nothing could go wrong.

questions.prompt: Why did she test the volcano in the kitchen?
options: She wanted her mother to see it.
questions.explanation: She tested it in the kitchen because it was raining outside.

questions.prompt: What did she do that caused the problem?
options: She used too much baking soda.
questions.explanation: She decided the volcano was not big enough and added another cup of vinegar.

questions.prompt: How did her mother react?
questions.explanation: She was not angry and even helped to clean up.

questions.prompt: What happened at the competition?
options: The judges did not like the volcano.
questions.explanation: She took a smaller volcano, it worked perfectly, and she came second.

parts.title: The story of the light bulb
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Today we take electric light for granted, but just 150 years ago, most people used candles or oil lamps in the evening. [1] The idea of a light bulb was not new, and many inventors had tried to make one.

In the 1870s, two men were working on the problem, one in England and one in the United States. [2] Their bulbs were very different from those we have now, and they did not last long.

The American inventor, Thomas Edison, tested thousands of materials to find the best thread for his bulb. [3] Finally, he found that a thin thread made of cotton and burned in a special way could give light for over a thousand hours.

However, a light bulb is not much use without electricity in the home. [4] It took many years before every town had power stations and wires to bring electricity to the houses.

Today, the old bulbs are being replaced by new ones, which are much cheaper to use. [5] Perhaps in a hundred years, our children will wonder how we managed with such wasteful lamps.
sentences: A single modern bulb can last for twenty years.
Edison also had to find a way to produce and supply the power.
Both of them came close to success.
Some of his tests failed after only a few minutes.
Candles are still popular for birthday cakes.
It was the invention of the light bulb that changed this.

gaps.explanation: "Most people used candles or oil lamps" is followed by the invention that changed this; the next sentence says the idea was not new.
Two men worked on the problem; "Both of them came close" continues, and the next sentence says their bulbs did not last long.
Edison tested thousands of materials; some failed within minutes, and "Finally" introduces the success.
A bulb needs electricity at home; the sentence about producing and supplying power leads to the many years before towns had power stations.
Old bulbs are being replaced by cheaper ones; a modern bulb lasting twenty years supports this, and the next sentence looks to the future.

parts.title: Robots at home
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Robots are no longer found only in factories. Today, many families have a small robot that cleans the floor while they are [1] work. These machines use sensors to [2] objects in the room, so they do not crash into the furniture. Some even know when the battery is low and [3] to their station. Scientists are now trying to build robots that can help older people to live [4] their own homes for longer. They could carry heavy bags, remind people to take their medicine, or call for help if somebody [5]. However, many people worry that robots will take away jobs. Experts say that the best idea is to let humans and machines [6] together, so that each does what it does best.

questions.prompt: Gap 2

questions.prompt: Gap 3

questions.prompt: Gap 4

questions.prompt: Gap 5

questions.prompt: Gap 6

parts.title: An email to a teacher
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage:
Dear Mr Hale,
I am writing to tell you about my project for the science fair. I would like to build a small machine [1] makes electricity from the wind. I have already bought most of the parts, but I still need [2] find a small motor. Could you tell me [3] there is one in the school lab? I would be very grateful if you could help, [4] I do not have much money. The fair is [5] the fifth of May, so I do not have much time. I promise to be careful, and I will wear goggles [6] all times.
Yours sincerely,
Winslow Pike

gaps.explanation: The relative pronoun refers to the machine.
"Need to find" is followed by the infinitive.
"Tell me if there is one" is an indirect yes/no question.
"Because" gives the reason why he needs help.
"At all times" is a fixed expression.

parts.title: An interview with an inventor
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Hildebrand, you invented a bicycle light that charges itself. How did the idea come to you?

turns.speaker: hildebrand
turns.text: I was cycling home in the dark one winter evening, and my battery light stopped working. I almost had an accident. I thought, why can't a light make its own power while I am pedalling?

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Was it easy to build?

turns.speaker: hildebrand
turns.text: Not at all. My first version was much too heavy, and it made a terrible noise. I worked in my parents' garage for two years, and I made more than fifty different models.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Did you ever want to give up?

turns.speaker: hildebrand
turns.text: Many times. Once I spent a whole summer on a model that did not work at all. But my sister told me that every mistake was a lesson, and that helped me to continue.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How did you find the money to start?

turns.speaker: hildebrand
turns.text: I entered a competition for young inventors and won a small prize. A local company then offered to make the lights and sell them. Today, we sell them in twelve countries.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What do you enjoy most about your work?

turns.speaker: hildebrand
turns.text: Seeing someone use something that I have made. Last month, I saw a girl riding past my window with my light on her bike. I felt very proud.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What would you say to young people who want to be inventors?

turns.speaker: hildebrand
turns.text: Look around you and ask what is annoying or difficult in everyday life. That's where the best ideas come from. And do not be afraid of failure.
